chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from the one who mentioned it, from Mufazzal al-Ju'fi, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'How ugly it is for a man that he is seen in the place of immorality, so that it is attributed to us and to the righteous of our companions. O Mufazzal! Do you know why it was said: 'The one who commits adultery, one day adultery will be committed with him'? I said, 'No, may I be sacrificed for you.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'There was a prostitute among the Children of Israel, and there was a man among the Children of Israel who used to frequently visit her. So when it was the end of his going to her, Allah caused to flow upon her tongue: 'Indeed, you will return to your family and you will find a man with her'.

He said: 'So he went out, and he was ill-tempered. So he entered his house in a manner different from the manner in which he used to enter before that day, and he used to enter with permission, so he entered that day without permission, and he found a man on his bed. So they raised the matter to Musa (peace be upon him)'.

So Jibraeel (peace be upon him) descended upon Musa (peace be upon him) and he said: 'O Musa! The one who commits adultery, one day adultery will be committed with him'. So he looked at the two of them and he said: 'Restrain, and your womenfolk will restrain'.

key_terms.عِفُّوا تَعِفَّ نِسَاؤُكُمْ: Restrain, and your womenfolk will restrain
key_terms.مَنْ يَزْنِ يَوْماً يُزْنَ بِهِ: The one who commits adultery, one day adultery will be committed with him

ai.seo_question: What is the story behind the saying 'The one who commits adultery, one day adultery will be committed with him'?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the proverb 'The one who commits adultery, one day adultery will be committed with him' by recounting a narrative from the Children of Israel, where a frequent visitor to a prostitute was divinely informed he would find a man with his wife. This incident, confirmed by the revelation to Prophet Moses (peace be upon him) via Gabriel, illustrates the principle of *ithar* (precedence) in divine retribution, where one's own actions create the precedent for similar consequences befalling them. This hadith is foundational in Shia jurisprudence and exegesis for understanding how individual sins can manifest as communal or personal trials.
